pages.title: The import page
pages.html:
The import page (uv run imagestream, or uv run imagestream-cli gui) sets up a project: one or more IDEAS exports, the names and roles of their channels, and the analysis settings. It runs the analysis and shows the overview. It is a page in your browser served by the program on your own computer; nothing leaves it.

The page remembers the last saved project (Save, Run and Quit save it); a setup that was not saved yet comes back from the browser after a reload, with a message. A second start opens the running page again. Quit (top right) saves the project and stops the program; otherwise it stops by itself 15 minutes after the page was closed (never during a run).

The ? button behind a step or a group of settings, and the ? Help button at the top, open the part of this manual about it in a panel at the side; F1 or ? does the same for the step under the mouse.

1. Project

The output folder of the project. Browse… chooses it, Open project… opens an existing project.toml, Save writes the project file without running. The results of a dataset go to <project>/<experiment>/<dataset>/.

2. IDEAS exports

Add zip files… (or paste a path and Add) adds exports. For each export:

  • Pixel size: 20×, 40× or 60× (1, 0.5 or 0.33 µm per pixel), or other…. IDEAS files do not contain it. Check it for your instrument: these are the nominal values.
  • Datasets: every first-level folder of the zip is a dataset. Use includes it; Objects counts the objects, Complete those that have every needed channel (the others are left out). Experiment groups datasets (it starts as the name of the zip): see Pools below.

  • Channels: the example images show a few objects of each channel. Give every needed channel a name; tick its role:

    Role Meaning How many
    BF brightfield one
    Tumor the tumor-cell marker one
    Immune an immune-cell marker; several are summed one or more
    Subtype an immune subtype marker: positive or negative per cell none or more
    MOI the marker of interest, measured along the membrane one, or none

    A channel can have two roles (for example a subtype marker that is also the marker of interest). Without a marker of interest the analysis gives the cell types, subtypes and contacts only: leave MOI unticked and Membrane profiles and enrichment off.

Copy setup to all gives the other exports the same pixel size and channel names. Remove removes the export from the project (not from disk).

Technical: roles go with the name

The roles are stored once for the project, by marker name ([channels] in project.toml), and every export only maps its channel numbers to names. So exports of the same panel whose channels are numbered differently (another instrument setup, another IDEAS template) need no other roles: only the right names. A tick box is greyed out until the channel has a name. Renaming a channel takes its roles along, unless another export still uses the old name.

Projects written before November 2026 stored the roles per export, by number. On opening, they become roles by name when all exports agree; otherwise each export keeps its own numbers (shown under its channel table).

3. Analysis settings

Used for all datasets of the project. The most important:

  • Tumor / immune markers: nuclear or membrane: where the tumor and immune markers stain, which decides how the image for Cellpose is made (see Segmentation).
  • Marker of interest expressed in: the cell type that carries the marker of interest. The membrane enrichment is measured on these cells (see Membrane enrichment).
  • Python with Cellpose, Model, Cell diameter (px): the segmentation. Sizes are in pixels: see Segmentation for the conversion from µm. Reuse the previous Cellpose result if nothing changed (on by default) skips Cellpose for a dataset whose Cellpose input and settings are the same as in its previous run.
  • Classify together, Threshold of the subtype markers, Artefact: the cell types. Thresholds set by hand lists the thresholds applied from a dashboard; Automatic again removes them.
  • Membrane profiles and enrichment, Membrane of, Interface with: the membrane enrichment.

All settings lists every setting with its default.

Pools

Classify together (one set of thresholds): experiment (the default) classifies the cells of all datasets with the same experiment label together, so that "positive for a marker" means the same in every dataset of the experiment; dataset classifies each dataset on its own. See Cell types.

4. Run

The list above Run all datasets names what is missing (an output folder, a pixel size, a channel for a role, …); the button works when the list is empty. The run saves the project first. The log follows the run; Stop ends it. A dataset that fails is logged and the others go on.

5. Overview

One row per analysed dataset, with a link to its dashboard and its folder. See The project overview.

pages.title: The dashboard
pages.html:
Every analysed dataset gets a dashboard.html in its folder. It opens from the overview of the import page, or directly from disk (double-click): it needs no server and no internet, so a folder can be sent to a colleague. The event images are in dashboard_files/ next to it.

Everything is linked: hovering a cell in the events, a plot or a table highlights it everywhere; clicking selects it and shows it in the Cell card. Esc clears the selection. dashboard.html#cell=12 or #event=5 in the address selects that cell (row of the cell table) or event when the page opens.

The page remembers its view (channels and their brightness, overlays, filter, sort, size, membrane pair and tabs) in the browser, per dashboard, and shows it again the next time it is opened.

Top: counts and filters

The header counts events, cells, cell types, events with one tumor and one immune cell, touching pairs, artefacts and cells with an interface. The filter row below applies to every view:

  • Events: all, those with immune and tumor cells, one tumor + one immune cell, those with an interface, those with touching cells. A contact chosen in the interaction matrix adds a chip here (✕ clears it).
  • Sort: the order of the events.
  • Size: the size of the event images; also Ctrl+scroll over the gallery. Small events show only their number (hover for the IDEAS object number).

The ? button behind a heading, and the ? Help button at the top, open the part of this manual about it in a panel at the side; F1 or ? does the same for the card under the mouse. The panel works offline.

Events

The events as a gallery, with the cells outlined in the colour of their type and the interfaces in aqua. Only the visible events are drawn, so large datasets stay fast.

Channels and overlays

The column left of the gallery switches what is drawn in the event images:

  • Channels: one row per channel, with a tick box and its brightness. Double-click a channel's name to show only that channel. Brightfield starts at half brightness, under the fluorescence.
  • Overlays: the outlines of the cells (in the colour of their type), the interfaces and the contacts: a white line, with a dark edge, between the centres of every two cells that touch.

Cell

The selected cell: its event, measurements, subtype markers (value, positive or negative), the cells it touches, and, with the membrane analysis, its membrane profile aligned on the interface.

Subtype markers

Shown when the panel has subtype markers. Per marker, a histogram of the immune cells (on a log scale: log(intensity − min + 1)), the threshold of the run (dashed; the numbers are background-subtracted intensities) and a slider. Where the histogram has two clear peaks, the threshold belongs in the gap between them (see Cell types). Dragging the slider changes the subtypes everywhere on the page at once: the colours, the plots, the contacts, the membrane pairs and the tables. The count next to the marker says how many immune cells are positive.

To make the thresholds of the sliders those of the tables and of every other output:

  • Apply to the project… (only in a dashboard opened from the overview of the import page): writes the thresholds that were moved, and the membrane pair if it was changed, into the project, and runs it again. Cellpose is skipped when its input and settings did not change, so this takes seconds per dataset; the page reloads when the run is done. The thresholds hold for all datasets of the project: the page asks first and says how many.
  • Copy as settings copies the thresholds and the membrane pair as lines for a settings file or project.toml to the clipboard (and shows them). This also works in a dashboard opened from disk.

A threshold set this way shows Run: manual under its slider, with an automatic button: on the next Apply the threshold is computed automatically again. The import page lists the thresholds set by hand (Analysis settings). Reset all returns the sliders to the run's thresholds.

Technical: what the slider changes, and what not

The slider re-applies the threshold to the immune cells in the page. It does not repeat the tumor / immune clustering, and the artefacts stay as computed: both would need the whole classification again (the artefact rule uses thresholds over all detections, see Cell types). In the run, a threshold set by hand (classification.thresholds) is used for both: for the subtypes and for the artefact rule.

So a threshold applied to the project can change the artefacts too, and with them the counts of the other cells.

Cell classes

Area against the marker ratio (immune / tumor marker), log–log: the space in which the k-means separates tumor cells from immune cells. Clicking a type in the legend brings it forward.

Marker of interest at the interface

Per event, the mean of the marker of interest at the interface against the rest of the membrane, for the cell type that expresses it (the per-event table of the Fiji macro). Points above the dashed line: more at the interface. Not shown without a marker of interest.

Interactions

  • Partner preference (left): rows are cell types, columns the type they touch. The colour and the number: contacts observed ÷ expected by chance, within the events of three or more cells (blue: fewer than chance, red: more). fraction touching shows instead the share of the row's cells that touch one of the column's type. Hovering a square gives the counts. Clicking a square shows only the events with that contact, with the contacts drawn.
  • Among immune cells (tab): the subset preference: per immune subtype, whether it is the one touching the tumor cell (or another subtype) more often than chance when an event offers a choice. Squares are coloured only where the 95 % interval excludes 1; hover for the counts and the interval.
  • Share of contacts (right): per cell type, whom it touches, as a share of its contacts or as numbers; on the right the share of its cells that touch any cell.

How contacts and chance are defined, and what they can and cannot tell, is in Cell contacts.

Membrane enrichment

Shown when the membrane analysis was run. Membrane of and interface with choose the pair: a cell type, an immune subtype, or all immune cells positive for a marker. The page computes the enrichment for that pair at once; Apply to the project… makes it the pair of the tables (see Subtype markers).

  • Histogram: the enrichment at the interface (aqua) of every cell with an interface, against random control windows on cells without an interface (dashed), in standard deviations above the mean of the free membrane.
  • Average profile: the profiles of the cells with an interface, centred on the interface.
  • Heatmap: one row per cell with an interface, the strongest on top.
  • All pairs (folded): the median enrichment of every Membrane of × interface with combination, with the number of cells and the marker check of each pair. Compare pairs here (see The control); clicking a number shows that pair.
  • The badge next to the menus: whether the marker of interest is on the measured cells, also on their partners, on both at a similar level, or hardly on the measured cells at all (grey: not informative). Read Membrane enrichment before trusting a result with an amber, red or grey badge, and The control on what the control windows can and cannot tell.
Technical: the page and the tables

The page computes the pair from every cell's membrane profile and neighbour track, as the program does for the tables. Only the random control windows differ (the page uses a fixed seed, the run an unseeded generator); their summaries agree closely. The tables (Membrane intensity analysis.tsv) hold the pair of the settings.

Tables

Cells, Events and Contacts, sortable by clicking a column header. Rows follow the filters; at most 2000 are shown (sort to see others). Download .tsv saves the current table with all its rows, as filtered and sorted here and with the subtypes of the sliders. The tables of the run are the TSV files in the output folder.

pages.title: The project overview
pages.html:
The last step of the import page shows one row per analysed dataset, and below it the partner preference of every experiment. The same is written to overview.tsv and interactions.tsv in the project folder.

The table

One row per dataset; dashboard opens the dataset's dashboard, folder its folder. A dataset that failed shows its error instead. Hovering a column header shows what it means:

Column Meaning
events, cells the events analysed; the cells after the clean-up, artefacts included
immune cells, tumor cells, artefacts the cell types (see Cell types)
single tumor + single immune cell events with exactly one tumor and one immune cell that touch
interactions pairs of touching cells, of any types
MOI partners / measured the marker check (see Membrane enrichment); empty without a marker of interest
marker check the marker check of the project's membrane pair, in words
tumor–immune contacts pairs of a tumor and an immune cell that touch
doublet fraction single tumor + single immune cell divided by events
median Tumor (or Immune) membrane ratio (doublets) in those events: the mean marker of interest in the measured cell's membrane band at the interface, over the rest of its band (the macro's ratio; all immune cells, whatever the membrane pair; no control, see the per-event table)
immune negative, immune A+, immune A+ B+, … immune cells with exactly that combination of positive subtype markers (immune A+ is negative for the other markers); 0 where a dataset has none
membrane pair the pair of the enrichment columns that follow: Membrane of … with …
membranes, with interface the measured cells of that pair, and those that touch a partner
median stdDevs above mean, median control (windows) the median enrichment of the cells with an interface, and of the control windows

The enrichment columns follow the membrane pair of the project: after Apply to the project… with another pair in a dashboard, they describe that pair. Note the pair with the numbers. Every other pair of every dataset is in membrane pairs.tsv in the project folder, without another run.

Partner preference per experiment

One matrix per experiment, for all its datasets together: contacts observed ÷ expected by chance, in the events of three or more cells (blue: fewer than chance, red: more). Hover a square for the counts. Comparing the matrices of experiments shows whether a preference holds across samples. Between immune subtypes, read the subset preference instead: this matrix also compares cells of different size (immune–immune ratios well below 1 appear without any preference), and it pools the datasets of the experiment, so it cannot show a difference between conditions within it. How it is computed, and what it does not measure, is in Cell contacts.

Technical: summing over datasets

interactions.tsv holds every dataset's contact table, and per experiment a row "(all)": the contacts, the cells touching and the expected contacts summed over its datasets, and observed / expected computed from those sums (not the mean of the datasets' ratios, which would weigh a small dataset as much as a large one).

pages.title: The output folder
pages.html:
The project folder

File Contents
project.toml the project: exports, channel names, roles and settings (see Settings files)
overview.tsv one row per dataset (the overview)
interactions.tsv the contact tables of all datasets, and summed per experiment
membrane pairs.tsv the membrane pairs of all datasets
subset preference.tsv the subset preference of all datasets (with intervals), and summed per experiment (without)
<experiment>/<dataset>/ the results of one dataset (below)

The folder of a dataset

Tables are tab-separated text (.tsv) with 3 decimals; NaN marks a value that does not exist (a mean of nothing). For an IDEAS export, the tables per cell and per event end with the column Object ID, the IDEAS object number.

File Contents
Cell classification.tsv one row per cell: measurements, cell type, subtype, neighbours (below)
All cell combinations.tsv one row per event: cells per type, marker of interest at the interfaces (left out without a marker of interest), whether a tumor and an immune cell touch (Tumor-immune interface), contacts
Single Tumor Single Immune cell.tsv the events with exactly one tumor and one immune cell that touch
Marker thresholds.tsv the threshold of every subtype marker, for the artefact rule and on the immune cells, in background-subtracted intensity (as Mean ch<N>), and how it was found (how)
Interactions.tsv contacts per cell type and neighbour type, with the comparison with chance
Membrane pairs.tsv every pair of Membrane of and Interface with: the cells with an interface, the median enrichment and ratio, the marker check (with the membrane analysis)
Subset preference.tsv per immune subtype and partner: contacts against the subtypes shuffled among the immune cells of each event, with the 95 % interval (with two or more immune subtypes)
Multiplets.tsv the number of events with n cells and with n contacts
Membrane intensity analysis.tsv one row per measured cell: interface and membrane means, enrichment, control
Average normalized membrane profile values - interfaces centered at 20.tsv the average aligned profile
Histogram_interface_stdDevs_above_mean.tsv, Histogram_control_stdDevs_above_mean.tsv the histograms
Control windows stdDevs above mean.tsv every random control window
membrane_profiles_normalized.tif the aligned profiles, one row per row of the membrane table
labelmap_cells.tif, labelmap_cells.json the labels as Cellpose made them (the montage), and what produced them: reused by the next run when nothing changed (see Segmentation)
labelmap_final.tif, labelmap_classes.tif the cleaned labels per event; the cell type per pixel (1 immune, 2 tumor, 3 artefact)
dashboard.html, dashboard_files/ the dashboard
settings.toml the complete settings of the run (channels by number)
run.json, summary.json, log.txt version, counts, Cellpose version and device, timing, the marker check; the log

The membrane files exist only when the membrane analysis was run.

The cell table

Column Meaning
Immune intensity, Tumor intensity mean of the normalized immune markers (summed) and tumor marker in the cell
Marker ratio, Marker ratio over Area immune / tumor intensity; the same divided by the area (the k-means uses these)
Area, Area (µm²) pixels; square micrometres
Class, Cell type 0 tumor, 1 immune, 2 artefact; Tumor, Immune, Artefact
Frame, Label the event (1-based) and the cell's label (unique in the dataset)
Edge 1: the cell is cut by the edge of its event image
Mean ch<N> (<name>) the mean of every loaded channel, minus the channel's background
<marker>+ 0/1 per subtype marker (with the threshold of the immune cells)
Positive markers the number of subtype markers the detection is positive in (the thresholds of the artefact rule)
Subtype the immune subtype ("A+ B+", "negative"); empty for other cells
Neighbours, Touching (labels), Neighbour types the cells it touches: how many, which (labels), and their types
Object ID the IDEAS object number of the event
Technical: names that differ from the Fiji macro

The macro v1.8 says T cell where this program says immune cell (as ClassifyCellTypes 2.8), because the immune side can be defined by several markers. Its table Single Tumor Single T cell is therefore Single Tumor Single Immune cell here, and its columns T-cell intensity, T cells, mean Tcell interface and T cell membrane ratio are Immune intensity, Immune cells, mean immune interface and Immune membrane ratio. The other columns keep the macro's names; new columns come after them.

pages.title: Input
pages.html:
IDEAS exports

The input is an export from IDEAS: a zip with one folder per dataset, and in it one image per object and channel, <object>_Ch<N>.ome.tif. Every object (an ImageStream event) becomes one image in the analysis, in the order of the object numbers, and the object number is kept with every result (Object ID).

Only the channels with a name are read. An object that misses one of them is left out (the log says how many).

Which objects are in the export is decided in IDEAS: the gates and the population that was exported. The analysis sees nothing else, which matters for the cell contacts.

Technical: image size, background and padding

IDEAS images differ in size per object. Every image is centred in the size of the largest one, and the border is filled with the channel's background: the median over the objects of each object's median. The background is also what is subtracted from the cell means (Mean ch<N>), and the lower end of the display in the dashboard. These are the same rules as ImageStreamCombiner (BioImaging-NKI), so an export read directly gives the same images as a Combiner stack.

The extent of every object's own image is kept, so that cells cut by the edge of their image can be found (Segmentation).

ImageStreamCombiner stacks

A .tif made by ImageStreamCombiner (one frame per event) can be analysed with a settings file (input.image). Channels are then numbered by their position in the stack.

Technical: what a Combiner stack lacks

A Combiner stack orders the events as the files were listed in the zip and drops the object numbers, so its results cannot be traced back to IDEAS objects, and "the first N events" are other events than in the export. The padding is recognised as the outer rows and columns that hold exactly the background in every channel.

Channels, roles and pixel size

Every channel that is needed gets a name and a role (brightfield, tumor marker, immune marker(s), subtype markers, marker of interest): see The import page. The pixel size (µm) is set per export; IDEAS files do not contain it. It converts areas to µm² and positions along the membrane to µm.

The first N events

Only the first N events analyses only the first N objects (by object number) of every dataset, for a quick test of the settings.

pages.title: Segmentation
pages.html:
The cells of every event are segmented with Cellpose, then cleaned up and measured.

The image for Cellpose

Cellpose gets one montage of all events of a dataset, side by side in an about-square grid, not every event on its own. Its input depends on Tumor / immune markers:

  • nuclear (the markers stain the nucleus or the cytoplasm): channel 1 is the local variance of the brightfield (which outlines the cells), channel 2 the sum of the normalized tumor and immune markers.
  • membrane: one image, the sum of the normalized markers and of the normalized brightfield variance.

Cell diameter (px) is the typical diameter in pixels; Model is cyto3 (Cellpose 3) or cpsam (Cellpose 4), or the path of a model of your own.

Technical: why a montage, and why a grid

A single ImageStream event, a few cells on an empty background, looks unlike the microscopy images that the Cellpose models are trained on; segmented one by one, the events gave worse masks and took longer. The Fiji macro put all events in one row; a grid of about the same height and width is about 30 % faster and gives nearly the same masks (median IoU about 0.97 with the row on validation data). Montage columns = the number of events gives the macro's row.

Normalization: each marker is divided by the median, over the events, of its Otsu threshold per event (as the macro). Several immune markers are each normalized and then summed.

Sizes in pixels

All sizes are in pixels of the export: a size in µm divided by the pixel size (1, 0.5 or 0.33 µm at 20×, 40× or 60×).

Pixel size 15 µm cell: diameter its area 25 µm cell: diameter its area
1 µm (20×) 15 px about 180 px 25 px about 490 px
0.5 µm (40×) 30 px about 700 px 50 px about 2000 px
0.33 µm (60×) 45 px about 1600 px 75 px about 4400 px
  • Cell diameter (px): with two cell types of different size, start between the two, closer to the smaller one, and check in the dashboard that large cells are not split and small ones not merged (or let Cellpose 3 estimate it: 0).
  • Min. / Max. cell size (px): areas after shrinking; keep the minimum well below the area of the smallest cells (about a third of it) and the maximum above the largest.
  • Membrane / interface width (px): empty (the default) is about 1.5 µm: 2 px at 20×, 3 px at 40×, 5 px at 60×. It is also the distance at which two cells count as touching (see Cell contacts).

Clean-up

  1. A cell that Cellpose drew across the border of two events in the montage is split into one cell per event.
  2. Shrink cells (px): the cells are shrunk from the background by this many pixels (not from each other).
  3. Min. / Max. cell size (px): cells outside the range, after shrinking, are removed.
Technical: details of the clean-up

The shrinking is a 4-connected binary erosion of all cells together, multiplied with the labels, as CLIJ2 does in the macro: touching cells stay touching, which the contacts and interfaces rely on. As in the macro, the size filter is only applied when the cells are shrunk (Shrink cells > 0). Labels are numbered 1…N in the order of the events; a cell's label is unique in the dataset and names it in the tables.

Cells at the image edge

A cell cut by the edge of its event's own image (not of the padded frame) gets Edge = 1 in the cell table. Leave out cells cut by the image edge removes them before the classification. Their area and outline are incomplete, and so is their membrane.

Measurements

Every cell is measured in every loaded channel: the mean minus the channel's background (Mean ch<N>), and its area in pixels and µm². The normalized tumor and immune markers give Tumor intensity and Immune intensity, used for the classification.

Running again without Cellpose

Every run keeps the Cellpose result of a dataset (labelmap_cells.tif) with a fingerprint of what produced it (labelmap_cells.json). The next run of the dataset skips Cellpose when the fingerprint is the same, and says so in the log; clean-up, measurements and everything after them are done again. So changing a threshold, the membrane pair or the clean-up settings (shrinking, cell sizes) costs no new segmentation. Reuse the previous Cellpose result if nothing changed (segmentation.reuse_labels) switched off always runs Cellpose.

With segmentation.method = "labelmap" in a settings file, the labels of another run (labelmap_cells.tif, or the macro's labelmap_cells.zip) are loaded instead of running Cellpose.

Technical: what the fingerprint covers

The fingerprint is a hash of the image given to Cellpose (the montage of brightfield and markers, so it covers the data, the channels, the number of events, the marker location and the montage columns) and of the model, the diameter, the flow and cell probability thresholds and the Python of Cellpose. The GPU setting is not part of it. Results of runs before this was added have no fingerprint, so their next run uses Cellpose once more.

pages.title: Cell types
pages.html:
Every detection becomes a tumor cell, an immune cell with its subtype, or an artefact, in two steps: first the lineage, tumor or immune; then, for the immune cells, the subtype markers.

Tumor or immune cell

The cells are split into two groups by k-means clustering on three values per cell: the tumor marker, the immune marker (both normalized, on a log scale) and the area. The group with the lower immune/tumor marker ratio is the tumor cells. This is the classification of the Fiji macro v1.8.

Technical: the clustering

Features: log(immune intensity), log(tumor intensity) and area, each scaled to mean 0 and SD 1 (sample SD). k-means with 2 clusters, 10 starts, seed 48 (the macro's seed; scikit-learn's k-means is not bit-identical to ImageJ's, but on well-separated data the result is the same: 100 % agreement on the validation data). The tumor cluster is the one with the lower sum of marker ratio over area, as the macro computes it (its comment says average; with clusters of unequal size the two can differ).

Several immune markers are summed after normalization, so the immune side can be defined by a panel (for example CD3 and CD56) instead of one marker.

Immune subtypes

Each subtype marker gets a threshold: an immune cell above it is positive for that marker. The combination of positive markers is its subtype, named after them: Subtype A+, Subtype A+ Subtype B+, or negative. The thresholds are automatic, or set by hand (classification.thresholds, or with the sliders in the dashboard).

Threshold of the subtype markers:

  • Two populations (default): looks for a second, positive population next to the negative cells and puts the threshold where a cell is as likely to belong to one as to the other. If there is no such population (the positive cells form a tail rather than a peak), the threshold is the upper noise limit of the negative cells. It copes with a small positive population close to a large negative one, the usual case for a subtype marker.
  • MaxEntropy (as ClassifyCellTypes 2.8): finds the split of the histogram with the most information on both sides.
  • MaxEntropy strict: the MaxEntropy threshold, raised where needed so that it lies at least two robust standard deviations above the middle of the negative cells. Fewer false positives, a few more missed positives.
  • Otsu: the split that best separates two populations of similar size.

Marker thresholds.tsv says for every threshold how it was found (column how).

Check every threshold on its histogram in the dashboard before reading subtype numbers. Where the negative and positive cells form two clear peaks, the threshold belongs in the gap between them; the automatic methods can miss it on either side (see the technical note). A threshold set in the gap with the slider and applied to the project (Apply to the project…) then holds for every output.

Technical: the thresholds

Intensities of markers are roughly log-normal, so the threshold is found on

x = ln(v - min v + 1)

of the background-subtracted cell means v, with ImageJ's auto-threshold on a 256-bin histogram of x (as setAutoThreshold("MaxEntropy dark") in 2.8), and transformed back: t = etx - 1 + min v. A cell is positive when v > t. The MaxEntropy, Otsu, Yen and RenyiEntropy methods are ported from ImageJ's AutoThresholder and give the same thresholds as Fiji (checked to 10⁻¹¹).

The thresholds are computed on the immune cells only. A subtype marker may also be expressed by tumor cells; thresholding it within the immune cells keeps them from shifting the threshold.

The automatic thresholds can be off in both directions. MaxEntropy often cuts in the upper tail of the negative population, so some negative cells are called positive (on synthetic data typically 10–20 % of them, or about ten cells per marker in a dataset of a few hundred immune cells); this creates small spurious subtypes such as A+ C+. On other data it cuts into the positive population instead (in a test at 60×, a quarter of the positive cells were missed, where Otsu found them all). MaxEntropy strict only raises the threshold. The thresholds are in Marker thresholds.tsv, in background-subtracted intensity (as Mean ch<N>).

Technical: Two populations, step by step

All on the log scale x above (one value per cell of the population: the immune cells; for the artefact rule the artefact rule).

  1. The negative cells. A kernel density estimate of x (Gaussian kernel; bandwidth 0.9 · min(s, mathrmIQR/1.34) · n-1/5, Silverman's rule; evaluated on 1024 points) has its highest peak at the mode m of the negative cells. Their spread is estimated from the lower side of the peak only, where positive cells do not reach: sigma = 1.4826 · mathrmmedian(m - x) over the cells with x le m (for a normal distribution this is its standard deviation). The noise limit is m + 2.5 sigma.
  2. A second population. A mixture of two normal distributions is fitted to x by expectation–maximization, started at the mode and at the largest value (deterministic). Its upper component counts as a positive population when it holds at least 0.5 % of the cells, its mean lies at least two pooled standard deviations from the lower one (Ashman's D ≥ 2), and its mean lies above the noise limit.
  3. The threshold. With a positive population: where the two weighted normal densities cross, between their means: above it a cell is more likely positive than negative. It is never lower than m + 2sigma. Without one: the noise limit. Fewer than ten cells: MaxEntropy.

how in Marker thresholds.tsv reports which case applied, with the fraction of the fitted positive population: two populations (12 % positive): crossing, ... raised to mode + 2 SD, or no second population: noise limit.

Why. A threshold that maximizes a criterion over the whole histogram (Otsu, MaxEntropy) is pulled into the large negative population when the positive one is small, which is the common case for a subtype marker; a fixed distance above the negative cells ("strict") is right when there is no clear second population but cuts into a positive population that lies close. The two steps cover both. The method was chosen on simulated data: 600 cells, log-normal negative cells with noise (two spreads), positive cells 2–40 % of them and 3–40 times as bright, five repeats (500 samples). Total errors (false + missed positives) against the best possible threshold of each sample: best 2417, Two populations 4790, the noise limit alone 6825, MaxEntropy strict 14 881, Otsu 21 132, MaxEntropy 21 965. Almost all remaining errors are in samples where the two populations overlap (positive cells 2–5 % and at most 5 times as bright), where no threshold separates them. On the four user-test datasets (2289 positive cells in all), Two populations made 4 errors, MaxEntropy 286.

Limits. When the positive cells are a continuous tail, the noise limit decides, and the count depends on 2.5 SD: set the threshold by hand if the histogram shows a clearer place. A bimodal negative population (two batches of differently stained cells pooled) can be taken for two populations: classify such datasets separately (Classify together = dataset).

Technical: why two steps, and not one clustering of all cells

One k-means of all cells into k types was considered and not used: k-means favours groups of similar size and spread, so a small subtype is absorbed by a large neighbour; k must be chosen in advance; and the clusters must be named afterwards. A threshold per marker can be read, checked on its histogram and changed, and the combinations of positive markers name the subtypes directly.

Artefacts

A detection that is positive in all subtype markers (with two or more of them) is not taken to be a cell but an artefact, for example debris or a dead cell that takes up every dye. Artefacts are left out of the tumor/immune clustering, drawn in grey, and not counted as cells in the counts and the interfaces. Artefact: positive in at least N subtype markers sets another number; 0 switches the rule off.

The images cannot tell an artefact from a real cell that is positive for every marker. If such cells are expected, look at the artefacts in the dashboard (they are drawn in grey) before switching the rule off: with the rule off, real artefacts appear as a subtype positive for every marker, and are counted and take part in the contacts like cells. With one subtype marker the rule is off and an artefact counts as a positive immune cell (the log says so); check the positive cells by eye.

Technical: the artefact rule

The rule needs the subtype thresholds of the immune cells, which are only known after the tumor/immune clustering, which in turn should run without the artefacts. So the clustering runs twice:

  1. a first k-means of all detections finds the immune cells;
  2. every subtype marker is thresholded on those immune cells (the threshold method of the project, or the threshold set by hand); a detection positive in at least N markers by these thresholds is an artefact (Positive markers in the cell table holds the count; Marker thresholds.tsv: the rows "artefact rule");
  3. the final k-means runs on the other detections, and the subtype thresholds are computed again on its immune cells (the rows "immune cells"), which may differ slightly.

Until November 2026 the thresholds of the rule were computed over all detections. For well-separated markers they lay at the noise of the many negative cells (tumor cells included), so a cell positive for one marker that touched a cell positive for another picked up a little of its neighbour's light and became an artefact. In a test with three subtype markers, 5 of 47 "artefacts" were such cells; with the immune-cell thresholds the rule found exactly the 42 artefacts that were drawn.

Only the subtype markers count. Counting the tumor and immune markers as well (a detection bright for both could be two cells drawn as one) was tried and dropped: an automatic threshold of those markers over all detections calls far more cells positive than the clustering finds, so most detections would become artefacts.

Several datasets: pools

With Classify together = experiment (the default), the cells of all datasets with the same experiment label are classified together: one clustering and one set of thresholds. A cell that is "Subtype A+" is then positive by the same standard in every dataset of the experiment, so the subtype fractions can be compared between datasets. With dataset, each dataset gets its own thresholds.

Technical: when to pool

Pool datasets that were stained and acquired alike (an experiment). Each dataset keeps its own background and its own normalization of the tumor and immune markers; only the clustering and the thresholds are shared. Datasets of different staining batches or instrument settings can differ in brightness: give them different experiment labels, or classify per dataset. The run then measures all datasets first, classifies each experiment, and finishes each dataset; run.json says what a dataset was classified with.

Colours

The dashboard colours up to eight cell types apart (tumor, up to six immune types, artefacts), in a fixed order so that a type keeps its colour when others come and go. More immune types share a grey; the legends and tables always name the types.

pages.title: Cell contacts
pages.html:
Which cells touch

Two cells of the same event touch when one comes within Membrane / interface width of the other (empty, the default: about 1.5 µm, i.e. 2 px at 20×, 3 px at 40×, 5 px at 60×): the same distance that defines the interfaces. So a cell with an interface always lists its partner among the cells it touches. Cells in different events never touch.

Every cell lists the cells it touches (Touching (labels)) and their types (Neighbour types); every event counts its pairs (Interactions).

Technical: the distance

"Within k pixels" means k steps between 4-connected pixels: the reach of the dilation that makes the interfaces (as CLIJ2 in the macro). Two cells with no background pixel between them are 1 step apart; with a gap of g pixels, g + 1. ClassifyCellTypes 2.8 used MorphoLibJ's region adjacency graph on the shrunk labels, which counts only cells that touch directly; here cells that almost touch also count, as they do for the interfaces.

The default is set in µm, not in pixels, so that "touching" means the same at every magnification: the number of pixels nearest 1.5 mumathrmm / pixel size, at least 2. A fixed 3 px meant 3 µm at 20× (near misses counted as contacts) and 1 µm at 60×. A width set in pixels is used as it is.

Counting contacts

Interactions.tsv (and the dashboard) count, per cell type and the type it touches:

  • contacts: the touching pairs; a pair of A and B counts once in row A and once in row B;
  • cells touching: the cells of the row's type that touch at least one cell of the column's type, and that fraction of the row's cells.

Partner preference: contacts compared with chance

Plain counts mostly reflect how many cells of each type there are. To see whether some types prefer each other, the contacts are compared with chance: the contacts expected if the cell types were shuffled among the cells of each event, with the cells of every event and its number of contacts kept as they are. The ratio observed / expected is above 1 when two types touch more often than random pairing of the cells in their events would give, and below 1 when they touch less often.

Only events of three or more cells take part. In an event of two touching cells, the pair can only be the pair it is: observed and expected are equal by construction, whatever the biology. Such events would pull every ratio towards 1, so they are left out of the comparison (they still count in the plain contacts). The dashboard says how many pairs that leaves.

Technical: the expected contacts, exactly

No random shuffling is done: the expectation is computed exactly. In an event of n cells, of which cA are of type A, a given touching pair consists of an A and a B cell (A ≠ B) with probability

pAB = (2 cA cB) / (n (n-1))

and of two A cells with probability cA (cA - 1) / (n (n-1)). The expected contacts of A with B are the sum over the events of three or more cells of (number of pairs) × pAB, counted from both sides as the observed ones (an A–A pair twice). So the page and Interactions.tsv give identical numbers, and type pairs that never touch but would by chance also get a row (observed 0: avoidance).

The sum of the expected contacts equals the sum of the observed ones: chance only redistributes the contacts over the types.

What the selection in IDEAS means

The export contains the objects that were selected in IDEAS: often only multiplets, without single cells, and sometimes only events with both cell types. The comparison with chance accounts for which cells are in each event (it shuffles only within the event), but not for why an event was exported. So it answers:

Within the exported multiplets of three or more cells, which cell types touch each other more, or less, than random pairing of the cells in their events would give?

It does not answer how often immune cells bind tumor cells in the sample: that needs the cells that never touched (the singlets) and the events without contacts, which are not in the export. A conjugate frequency ("the percentage of T cells in conjugates") can only be computed from an export that keeps all events, singlets included.

Technical: further limits of the null model
  • The model treats every pair of cells in an event as equally likely to touch. In reality, large cells have more room for neighbours than small ones, so in an event with one large and several small cells the large cell takes part in more contacts than chance gives it. Comparing the same cell types between conditions is safer than reading one ratio on its own.
  • Small numbers make large ratios: a ratio of 2 from 2 observed and 1 expected contact means little. The tooltip in the dashboard and the table give the counts; look at them.
  • Artefacts take part like cells; with a stricter artefact rule they move to the cell types, and back.
  • With no preference at all, tumor–tumor came out at about 1.5 in tests (larger cells, more neighbours), and real preferences come out weaker than they are: in a test, a subset placed next to tumor cells far more often after a treatment rose only from 1.03 to 1.11, consistently in both donors. Compare datasets (donors, conditions) with each other rather than a ratio with 1.

Subset preference: which immune cells touch

The partner preference above shuffles all cell types, and so compares tumor cells with immune cells, which differ in size. For the immune subtypes a cleaner question is: when an event offers a choice of immune cells, is the one that touches the tumor cell (or another immune cell) more often of this subtype than chance? For this only the subtypes are shuffled, among the immune cells of each event; the cells, their positions, the tumor cells and the contacts stay as they are. Only events with at least two immune cells take part: with one immune cell there is no choice.

The result is observed / expected per subtype and partner (tumor cells or a subtype), with a 95 % interval; with fewer than 5 contacts expected there is no interval. In the dashboard (Interactions, tab among immune cells) only squares whose interval excludes 1 are coloured. Many squares are tested at once: one square out of twenty excludes 1 by chance alone, so trust a preference that holds in every dataset (donor, replicate), not one square. The tables are Subset preference.tsv per dataset and subset preference.tsv in the project folder.

Technical: the subset preference, exactly

Expected. In an event with n immune cells, cS of subtype S, every immune cell has subtype S with probability cS / n when the subtypes are shuffled among them. So each immune–tumor contact of the event is one of subtype S with that probability, and each immune–immune contact is one of subtypes S and T with probability 2 cS cT / (n (n − 1)), or S and S with probability cS (cS − 1) / (n (n − 1)), counted from both sides as in the contact table. The expected contacts are these probabilities summed over the contacts of all events with n ≥ 2; observed are the contacts counted in the same events (contacts). Artefacts take no part; tumor cells are never shuffled.

The interval. The events are resampled with replacement (as many as there are), observed and expected are summed again, and observed / expected is recomputed; the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles over 1000 resamples (Python, seeded, so the tables are reproducible) or 400 (the page; slightly different) are the interval. It reflects the sampling of events within one dataset, not the variation between donors: compare datasets for that. Below 5 expected contacts no interval is given: a resample of a handful of contacts often contains the same contacts every time, which gives an interval of zero width that excludes 1 on one or two contacts.

Why within events. Shuffling the subtypes over the whole dataset asks whether a subtype is over-represented among the immune cells that touch tumor cells. In an export of conjugates nearly every immune cell touches a tumor cell (95 % in the example data), so that ratio can hardly exceed about 1.05 whatever the biology. Within an event with a choice it can. In the example data (Subtype A+ cells were placed next to the tumor cell more often) the dataset-wide version gave 1.00 (0.93–1.08), the within-event version 1.09 (1.03–1.17). Effects are small in both because most events offer little choice: one tumor cell with two immune cells usually lets both touch it.

What it does not remove. A subtype that is larger, or more often segmented as two cells, still touches more; subtypes are assumed to be of similar size. The selection in IDEAS applies as above.

Comparing conditions

The experiment label does two things: datasets with the same label are classified together (one threshold per marker, see pools), and the overview sums them into one partner-preference matrix. To compare, for example, control and treated samples stained in the same way:

  • give them one experiment label, so that "positive for A" means the same in both (or set the thresholds by hand);
  • compare the conditions per dataset: every dataset's own table is in interactions.tsv and subset preference.tsv (and in the dataset folders), with the observed and expected contacts; look at the same ratio in every donor, and at the counts behind it. A change that goes the same way in every donor is the result; the overview's matrix per experiment pools the conditions and cannot show it.
  • expect small numbers: few events give the immune cells a choice, so real changes of preference come out weak. In a test where a subset was placed next to the tumor cell more than twice as often after treatment, the ratio rose by 0.05–0.25, in the data's own geometry by about as much: the tool cannot recover more than the events contain.

Multiplets

Multiplets.tsv counts the events with n cells and with n contacts (n = 0, 1, 2, …), as the multiplets table of ClassifyCellTypes 2.8.

pages.title: Membrane enrichment
pages.html:
The question: is the marker of interest enriched in the membrane of one cell type where it touches another, compared with the rest of its membrane? Membrane profiles and enrichment switches this analysis on.

The membrane profile

For every cell, the outline is traced, smoothed, and straightened: the marker of interest is sampled in a band across the outline (Straightening width: about 4.5 µm, i.e. 5 px at 20×, 9 px at 40×, 13 px at 60×), and the brightest sample across the band is kept at every position. This gives a profile along the membrane, one value per pixel of perimeter, background-subtracted.

Along the same line, every position records whether another cell is within the interface width, and which one: the cell's neighbour track.

Technical: one membrane per cell

The Fiji macro straightened one ring per blob of touching cells of the same type; here every cell has its own membrane, so two touching tumor cells are two membranes. The outline runs along the pixel edges (marching squares), smoothed with a Gaussian (σ = 2 samples) where Fiji fits a spline, and resampled at 1 px. The neighbour track takes, at every own pixel within the interface width of another cell, the label of the nearest other cell. The length of every profile is kept; a value of 0 is data, not the end of the profile (in the macro, zeros ended it).

Technical: the straightening width, and a false enrichment it prevents

The outline that Cellpose draws lies a little outside the stained membrane where a cell is free (by about 1 µm in the tests, after Shrink cells), but on the contact line where two cells touch. The band across the outline must reach the membrane in both places. With a band that is too narrow, the brightest sample at the free membrane misses part of the membrane, while at a contact it does not: the interface then looks enriched for any membrane marker, with no biology.

In a test at 40× (0.5 µm per pixel; a ligand on the tumor membrane, enriched only where Beta+ immune cells touch), the tumor cells' interface with Beta− cells, which has no enrichment, measured:

Straightening width Beta− contacts (truth: none) Beta+ contacts (truth: enriched)
5 px (2.5 µm; the macro's value) 1.4–1.6 SD, ratio 1.31 7.2–7.5 SD, ratio 2.5–2.65
9 px (4.5 µm) 0.35 SD, ratio 1.05 6.5–6.7 SD, ratio 1.95–2.0
13 px (6.5 µm) 0.2 SD, ratio 1.03 6.6–7.1 SD, ratio 1.9

So the default is about 4.5 µm: the odd number of pixels nearest 4.5 mumathrmm / pixel size, at least 5. A wider band lowers the ratio of a real enrichment somewhat (the free membrane is now measured at its true brightness) but keeps it clearly apart. A width set in pixels (membrane.straightening_width) is used as it is; the comparison with the Fiji macro uses its 5 px.

A wider band also reaches further into a touching partner. That matters only when the partner carries the marker (see Where the marker is expressed).

A pair of cell types

Membrane of and Interface with choose the pair. Each can be a cell type (Tumor, Immune), an immune subtype as named in the tables (Immune Subtype A+, or Immune negative for the immune cells negative for every subtype marker), or a marker (Subtype A+: every immune cell positive for it, whatever its other markers). Empty: the cells that express the marker of interest (Marker of interest expressed in) against the other type, as in the macro. In the dashboard the pair can be changed on the spot.

For the measured cells, the interface is the part of the membrane whose neighbour track shows a partner; the free membrane is the part that touches no cell at all.

The enrichment

Per measured cell with an interface:

  • interface Mean and non-interface Mean: the mean of the profile at the interface and on the free membrane, and their ratio;
  • stdDevs above mean: how far the interface lies above the free membrane, in standard deviations of the free membrane:

SD above mean = (interface - free) / (SD(free))

The profiles are normalized the same way and aligned so that the centre of the longest interface lies at position 20; their average (cells with an interface only) shows the shape of the enrichment.

Technical: why the free membrane is the baseline

The macro compared the interface with the rest of the membrane, including the parts that touch other cells. A contact with another cell that carries the marker (for example two tumor cells, when the marker is on tumor cells) places two membranes side by side and is brighter; it would raise the baseline and lower the enrichment. Here the baseline is the membrane that touches no cell. On validation data this raised the median enrichment by about 0.2 SD; the control stayed the same.

The control

Cells without an interface get control windows: Control windows per cell (10) windows at random positions on their free membrane, as long as the median interface, scored like an interface. The histogram of the controls shows how much a stretch of free membrane varies by chance in this dataset.

The control windows are not a control for the interface itself. They lie on free membrane, so they cannot show what the contact does to the measurement regardless of the marker: two stained membranes side by side (see below), an outline that runs a little outside the membrane where the cell is free but not at a contact, or blur from the partner. In a test on synthetic data without any enrichment, the outline effect alone gave a ratio of about 1.3 and 1–1.5 SD with the macro's straightening width, and very small p-values against the control windows; the default width now removes most of it (see the technical note on the straightening width), but not the other effects. So:

  • Compare pairs, not an interface with the control windows: the same measured cells with partners that do carry a receptor or ligand and partners that do not (for example Immune A+ against Immune negative), or cells whose marker you expect to be enriched against cells of the same type (Interface with the measured type itself). The dashboard shows all pairs at once (All pairs in the membrane card): in the example below, the tumor cells' membrane is enriched only at contacts with Subtype A+ cells.

  • A small shift (ratio below about 1.5, or 1–2 SD) is within what geometry alone can give; a large, pair-specific effect is not.

  • Check in the dashboard that the outlines lie on the membrane (Events, overlay outlines).
  • The p-value of thousands of cells against thousands of windows says nothing about biological replicates: compare datasets (donors, replicates) instead.
Technical: comparing pairs, and why there is no reference channel

The pair table. For every selection under Membrane of (rows) and every cell type or subtype under Interface with (columns), the dashboard computes the median SD above mean of the measured cells that have an interface with that partner, exactly as for the chosen pair but without the control windows, and the number of such cells. A pair whose measured cells or partners do not carry the marker is the geometry-matched control of a pair that does: same cells, same kind of contact, same segmentation. Contacts between cells of the same type are the control for two stained membranes side by side: their enrichment is what doubling alone gives. Each entry carries the marker check of its pair (! partners carry part of the marker or as much, !! more, – the measured cells hardly carry it).

No reference channel. A second channel measured like the marker of interest, one that should not be enriched, looked like a natural control. The cells' own tracker dye was tested as such a reference in the 40× test above: being cytoplasmic, it fills the band at a contact but not at the free edge, and showed 4.8 SD (5 px) and 2.7 SD (9 px) of "enrichment". A reference must be stained like the marker (a membrane stain on the same cells), which a panel rarely has; the pair comparison needs no extra channel.

Technical: the control windows

The windows are drawn on the free membrane only, read as one closed line, and scored against the rest of that free membrane. The macro used one window of 25 px per membrane; many windows of the typical interface length estimate the null distribution better. The windows are random and not seeded, so the control differs slightly from run to run (the dashboard uses a fixed seed). All windows are in Control windows stdDevs above mean.tsv.

Where the marker is expressed

The marker of interest must be on the measured cells, not on their partners. At an interface, the membranes of the two cells lie against each other. If the partner carries the marker too, its membrane is measured along with the measured cell's, and the interface looks enriched even when both cells are stained evenly.

The analysis checks this. It compares the median free-membrane intensity of the partners with that of the measured cells, and reports it in the log, run.json, the overview (MOI partners / measured) and as a badge in the dashboard:

Partners / measured Badge Meaning
below 25 % ✓ green the marker is mainly on the measured cells
25–80 % ! amber the partners carry part of it: part of the interface signal may be theirs
80–125 % ! amber the marker is on both at a similar level: two stained membranes side by side look like enrichment; compare with contacts between cells of the same type
125 % or more ! red the marker is brighter on the partners: check Marker of interest expressed in and the pair
(any) – grey the measured cells hardly carry the marker (below 25 % of the brightest cell type): their enrichment is not informative
Technical: the marker check, exactly

For every cell its free-membrane intensity: the mean of its straightened profile where its neighbour track shows no cell (background-subtracted; without the membrane analysis the mean of the whole cell). Measured and partners are the medians over the cells of each selection; the brightest cell type is the highest median over the cell types and immune subtypes (artefacts excluded). In this order: partners / measured ≥ 125 %: brighter on the partners (red); measured below 25 % of the brightest type: not informative (grey); 80–125 %: on both (amber); 25–80 %: the partners carry part (amber); below 25 %: mainly on the measured cells (green). The bands are rules of thumb: at 25 % the partner adds a quarter of the measured cell's membrane signal to every interface pixel it reaches; at 80–125 % an interface between two equally stained membranes looks like a doubling whatever the biology.

If the badge is amber or red, choose the pair the other way round (if the marker is on the partners), compare the enrichment with that of a pair whose partners do not carry the marker, or treat the result as an upper bound.

Look at the subsets, on both sides. The default pair (all cells of the type that expresses the marker, with all cells of the other type) can hide an effect that only one subset has: in a test, a receptor polarized strongly on A+ immune cells gave a median of 0.2 SD over all immune cells, and a ligand enriched only where B+ cells touch gave 0.7 SD with all immune cells. The All pairs table of the dashboard and Membrane pairs.tsv give every combination of Membrane of and Interface with at once; read them before concluding that there is no enrichment.

Technical: inside only, and why it is no cure

Straighten inside the measured cell only takes the brightest sample only from the part of the band that lies inside the measured cell, so the band does not reach into the partner. This is a sensitivity test, not a separation: touching membranes are nanometres apart, far below the resolution of the ImageStream, so the blur mixes both membranes in every pixel near the interface, whichever pixels are sampled. If the enrichment drops clearly with inside only, part of it comes from the partner side; if it stays, that is reassuring but not proof.

The per-event table

Independently of the profiles, every event gets the mean of the marker of interest at the interface and on the rest of the membrane of each cell type (All cell combinations.tsv; for the events with one tumor and one immune cell, Single Tumor Single Immune cell.tsv), as in the macro. These use the membrane band of each cell type (Membrane / interface width) rather than the straightened profiles.

This is the macro's measure, and it has none of the safeguards above: it takes all partners of the other type together, has no control, and does not follow the membrane pair. A partner that carries the marker, or two stained membranes side by side, raise it as much as a real enrichment does (in a test without any enrichment it was 1.27). The overview's median … membrane ratio (doublets) and the dashboard card Marker of interest at the interface show it; read them together with the marker check, and use the pair comparisons for conclusions.

pages.title: All settings
pages.html:
Every setting, as it is written in a settings file or project.toml ([section], name = value), with its default and, where it has one, its label on the import page. A channel is given by number or by name.

[input]

The input: the export or stack, the dataset, its channels and pixel size.

Setting Default On the import page Meaning
image (none) an IDEAS export (.zip, one folder per dataset) or an ImageJ hyperstack from ImageStreamCombiner (.tif, one frame per event)
output 'output' the results go to a folder named after the dataset (or stack) in this folder
max_events (empty) Only the first N events (empty = all) analyse only the first N events (by object number); empty = all
dataset (empty) IDEAS zip: the dataset (folder in the zip); empty = the only one
channels [] IDEAS zip: the channels to load (IDEAS numbers Ch<N>); the channels with a role are always loaded
channel_names [] IDEAS zip: their names, in the same order as channels
pixel_size (empty) µm per pixel; required for an IDEAS zip (its files do not hold it)

[channels]

The roles of the channels (by number or by name).

Setting Default On the import page Meaning
brightfield 1 the brightfield channel
marker_of_interest 2 the marker whose enrichment at the interface is measured; empty ("") = none (only cell types and contacts; the membrane analysis needs one)
tumor 3 the tumor-cell marker
immune [4] the immune-cell marker(s), a list; several are each normalized and summed (2.8: phenotypic markers)
functional [] immune subtype markers, a list: positive or negative per immune cell (2.8: functional markers)
marker_location 'nuclear' Tumor / immune markers where the tumor and immune markers stain: "nuclear" (nucleus or cytoplasm) or "membrane"; sets the image for Cellpose
cell_of_interest 'Immune cell' Marker of interest expressed in the cell type that expresses the marker of interest: "Tumor cell" or "Immune cell"

[segmentation]

Cellpose and the clean-up of the cells.

Setting Default On the import page Meaning
method 'cellpose' "cellpose", or "labelmap": load the labels of labelmap_file instead
labelmap_file (empty) labelmap_cells.tif (or the macro's .zip) of an earlier run
model 'cyto3' Model (cyto3, cpsam, or a path) Cellpose 3: cyto3, cyto2, nuclei, ...; Cellpose 4: cpsam; or the path of a model
diameter 30.0 Cell diameter (px) the typical cell diameter in pixels; 0 = Cellpose estimates it (Cellpose 3 only)
flow_threshold 0.5 Cellpose's flow threshold (higher: more, less certain cells)
cellprob_threshold 0.0 Cellpose's cell probability threshold (lower: larger cells)
use_gpu true Use the GPU run Cellpose on the GPU
reuse_labels true Reuse the previous Cellpose result if nothing changed reuse the Cellpose result of the previous run of the dataset when its input image and Cellpose settings are the same (labelmap_cells.tif and .json in the dataset folder); off = always run Cellpose
montage_columns 0 Montage columns (0 = square) events per row of the montage that Cellpose segments; 0 = about square; the number of events = one row, as the Fiji macro
cellpose_python (empty) Python with Cellpose python.exe of an environment with Cellpose 3 or 4; empty = this one
erosion 1 Shrink cells (px) shrink the cells from the background by this many pixels
min_cell_size 100 Min. cell size (px) smaller cells (in pixels, after shrinking) are removed
max_cell_size 10000 Max. cell size (px) larger cells (in pixels, after shrinking) are removed
exclude_edge_cells false Leave out cells cut by the image edge leave out cells cut by the edge of their event image (they are always marked: column Edge)

[classification]

Subtype thresholds, artefacts and pools.

Setting Default On the import page Meaning
threshold_method 'Two populations' Threshold of the subtype markers the automatic threshold of the subtype markers, on log(intensity - min + 1): "Two populations" (where a positive population is as likely as the negative one, or the upper noise limit of the negative cells when there is no second population), "MaxEntropy" (as 2.8), "MaxEntropy strict" (at least 2 robust SDs above the negative cells) or "Otsu"; in a settings file also "Yen" or "RenyiEntropy"
thresholds {} Thresholds set by hand (Apply in a dashboard) thresholds set by hand, by marker name: { "Subtype A" = 12.5 } (background-subtracted intensity); they replace the automatic ones
artefact_min_positive (empty) Artefact: positive in at least N subtype markers (0 = none) a detection positive in at least this many subtype markers is an artefact, not a cell; empty = all of them (with two or more markers); 0 = no artefacts
pool 'experiment' Classify together (one set of thresholds) in a project: "experiment" classifies the datasets of each experiment together (one set of thresholds), "dataset" each dataset on its own

[membrane]

The membrane profiles and the enrichment.

Setting Default On the import page Meaning
analysis false Membrane profiles and enrichment the membrane profiles and the enrichment at the interface (the per-event interface table is always made)
cells [] Membrane of (e.g. Tumor, Immune, A+; empty = where the marker is expressed) the cells whose membrane is measured, a list of: a cell type ("Tumor", "Immune"), an immune subtype as in the tables ("Immune A+ B+"), or a marker ("A+": immune cells positive for A); empty = channels.cell_of_interest
partners [] Interface with (empty = the other cell type) the partners whose contact is the interface, as for cells; empty = the other cell type
thickness (empty) Membrane / interface width (px) pixels: the width of the membrane band, and the distance at which cells touch; empty = about 1.5 µm (2 px at 20x, 3 at 40x, 5 at 60x)
straightening_width (empty) Straightening width (px) pixels: the width of the band across the outline that is straightened; empty = about 4.5 µm (5 px at 20x, 9 at 40x, 13 at 60x), so that the band reaches the membrane where the outline lies a little outside it
max_histogram_value 20.0 Histogram maximum (SD) the end of the histograms (SD above the mean); they start at -5
histogram_bin_width 0.25 Histogram bin width (SD) the bin width of the histograms (SD)
control_repeats 10 Control windows per cell random control windows per cell without an interface, each as long as the median interface
inside_only false Straighten inside the measured cell only take the profile only from the part of the band inside the measured cell (a sensitivity test, not a separation: touching membranes are far closer than the resolution, so every pixel there mixes both)

pages.title: Settings files and the command line
pages.html:
Everything the import page does can be done from a terminal, with a project file (several exports) or a settings file (one dataset). Both are TOML text files.

Commands

uv run imagestream-cli gui                          # the import page (also: uv run imagestream)
uv run imagestream-cli run-project D:\data\project  # all datasets of a project (project.toml or its folder)
uv run imagestream-cli run settings.toml            # one dataset with a settings file
uv run imagestream-cli run settings.toml --max-events 50
uv run imagestream-cli example-settings > settings.toml   # a settings file with every default

A settings file

One dataset: the sections [input], [channels], [segmentation], [classification] and [membrane]. Relative paths are relative to the settings file. An unknown setting is an error, so a typing error is not silently ignored. All settings lists them.

[input]
image = 'D:/data/example_export.zip'
dataset = 'Donor 1'
channels = [1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8]
channel_names = ['BF', 'Marker', 'Tumor', 'Immune', 'Subtype A', 'Subtype B']
pixel_size = 0.5
output = 'results'

[channels]
brightfield = 'BF'           # a channel by name (or by number: brightfield = 1)
marker_of_interest = 'Marker'
tumor = 'Tumor'
immune = ['Immune']
functional = ['Subtype A', 'Subtype B']
cell_of_interest = 'Tumor cell'

[segmentation]
cellpose_python = 'D:/envs/cellpose3/Scripts/python.exe'
diameter = 20.0

[membrane]
analysis = true

The run writes the complete settings it used to settings.toml in the dataset's folder, with the channels by number: a run can be repeated exactly with that file.

A project file

project.toml as the import page writes it: the panel ([channels], by name), the shared settings, and one [[zip]] per export with its datasets:

[channels]
brightfield = 'BF'
marker_of_interest = 'Marker'
tumor = 'Tumor'
immune = ['Immune']
functional = ['Subtype A', 'Subtype B']
cell_of_interest = 'Tumor cell'

[classification]
pool = 'experiment'

[[zip]]
path = 'D:/data/example_export.zip'
pixel_size = 0.5
channels = [1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8]
channel_names = ['BF', 'Marker', 'Tumor', 'Immune', 'Subtype A', 'Subtype B']

[[zip.dataset]]
name = 'Donor 1'
experiment = 'Example'
include = true
Technical: older files

Settings files from before November 2026 name the immune marker t_cell = 4 and the cell of interest 'T cell'; they are read as immune = [4] and 'Immune cell'. Older project files with roles per export, by number, are converted to roles by name when all exports agree (see The import page).

pages.title: From the Fiji macros
pages.html:
ImageStream Analysis for Python ports two Fiji macros of BioImaging-NKI/ImageStreamAnalysis:

  • Analyze_ImageStream_stack_2celltypes_+_membrane_intensity_analysis_1.8.ijm: tumor and T cells by k-means, the per-event interface measurements, and the membrane enrichment;
  • ClassifyCellTypes_2_8.ijm: several immune markers, immune subtypes by thresholds, the cells that touch, and a class of non-cells.

The port reads IDEAS exports directly (it replaces ImageStreamCombiner) and joins the two macros: the 1.8 analysis is the case "one immune marker, no subtype markers". It was validated against the output of the 1.8 macro: the cells and the per-event tables match to three decimals with 100 % class agreement, and the membrane analysis matches on its distributions. The port does not reproduce the macros exactly where they could be improved; the differences are below, and in detail in docs/SPEC.md of the repository.

Differences

Topic The macros This program Why
Input a Combiner stack the IDEAS zip, object numbers kept traceable to IDEAS; one step less
Cellpose montage one row of all events an about-square grid faster, same masks
Cells across two events in the montage one cell split per event each event is its own image
Names T cell immune cell the immune side can be a panel of markers
Immune markers one (1.8); summed raw values (2.8) several, each normalized, then summed markers of different brightness weigh alike
Clustering 1.8: normalized markers and area; 2.8: raw sums, functional markers added unnormalized 1.8's 2.8 added the functional markers without normalizing them (a mistake)
Subtype thresholds MaxEntropy on all cells (2.8) Two populations (or MaxEntropy, Otsu) on the immune cells tumor cells do not shift the threshold; MaxEntropy called noise positive or missed positive cells (see Cell types)
Non-cells "crap" class, switched off and not working artefacts: positive in all subtype markers —
Contacts region adjacency graph of the labels within the interface width agrees with the interfaces
Contacts against chance — partner preference in events of 3+ cells; subset preference among immune cells, with intervals new
Membranes one ring per blob of touching cells of a class one membrane per cell a cell is the unit
Straightening width 5 px about 4.5 µm (9 px at 40×) 5 px at 40× gave a false enrichment at every contact (see Membrane enrichment)
Baseline of the enrichment all membrane outside the interface the membrane that touches no cell contacts with other marked cells raise the baseline
Control one window of 25 px per membrane, unseeded 10 windows of the median interface length, on free membrane a better null distribution
Average profile all rings, also without interface cells with an interface rings without interface halve the peak
Pair of cell types the cell of interest against the other class any pair, also subtypes; checked for where the marker is —
Several images concatenated (2.8), background of the last image pools per experiment, each dataset its own background 2.8 used the background of the last image for all
Settings record settings.txt, incomplete the complete settings.toml —
Technical: what is kept exactly

The normalization of the markers (the median over the events of each event's Otsu threshold, with ImageJ's 8-bit histogram of float images), the brightfield variance filter (ImageJ's circular kernel), the erosion and dilation (CLIJ2's 4-connected steps), the k-means features and the rule that picks the tumor cluster, the per-event table and the doublet table are as in macro 1.8, so that results stay comparable. The ImageJ auto-threshold methods are ported exactly; they give Fiji's thresholds.

pages.title: Questions and problems
pages.html:
Setting up

The run button stays grey. The list above it says what is missing: an output folder, a pixel size, or a channel for a role in one of the exports. A role is a tick box next to a named channel; an export whose channel has another name (a typing difference) does not get the role.

"Cellpose failed". The log shows Cellpose's own message. Check Python with Cellpose: it must be the python.exe of an environment in which Cellpose is installed. Use the GPU off runs on the processor (much slower).

An export has objects without all channels. IDEAS can export objects with missing channels; they are left out, and the log says how many. Complete on the import page counts the objects that have all needed channels.

Results

Cells are missed or merged. Check Cell diameter (px) first: Cellpose works best when it matches the cells. For cells that stain the membrane rather than the cytoplasm, set Tumor / immune markers to membrane. Montage columns does not change much; leave it at 0.

Tumor and immune cells are swapped, or mixed. The k-means needs both cell types and markers that separate them. Look at Cell classes in the dashboard: two clouds should be visible. With very few cells of one type, the clustering can split the other type instead.

There are many artefacts. The automatic thresholds are liberal, so real cells can be positive in all subtype markers by chance. Look at the histograms in the dashboard; try MaxEntropy strict, set the thresholds by hand, or raise the number of markers in the artefact rule. See Cell types.

A rare subtype appears that should not exist (for example A+ C+ in a few cells). The automatic threshold of one of the markers probably lies in the noise of the negative cells. Look at the marker's histogram in the dashboard, drag the slider into the gap between the two peaks and Apply to the project…. See Cell types.

I only want cell types and contacts. Leave the MOI role unticked and Membrane profiles and enrichment off; the run then needs no marker of interest.

Does a subtype prefer the tumor cells? Look at the tab among immune cells in the dashboard's Interactions card: it compares the subtypes with each other within events, with a 95 % interval. See Cell contacts.

The partner preference is close to 1 everywhere. Most contacts may be in events of two cells, which cannot show a preference and are left out; the dashboard says how many pairs remain. With few events of three or more cells, the ratios are uncertain. See Cell contacts.

The membrane badge is amber or red. The partners carry the marker of interest too, and the interface may show their membrane. See Where the marker is expressed.

The control is not centred on 0. The control windows score random stretches of free membrane; with uneven staining along the membrane, the control spreads. The comparison that matters is the interface against the control of the same dataset.

The numbers differ slightly between two runs. The control windows are random (not seeded); everything else is the same for the same settings. The dashboard's control uses a fixed seed.

The dashboard

The dashboard is slow with many events. Only the visible events are drawn; the plots draw every cell. Filter the events, or analyse fewer events (Only the first N events) to test settings.

Can I send a dashboard to a colleague? Yes: send the dataset's folder (dashboard.html with dashboard_files/). It opens in any modern browser, without the program and without internet.

pages.title: Glossary
pages.html:
Artefact
A detection positive in all (or at least N) subtype markers: taken not to be a cell. Left out of the clustering and the counts of cells.
Background
Per channel, the median over the objects of each object's median intensity. Subtracted from the cell means.
Dataset
A folder in an IDEAS export: the objects of one sample. Analysed into a folder of its own.
Event
One object of the ImageStream: one image with one or more cells.
Experiment
A label that groups datasets: classified together (a pool) and summed in the overview.
Free membrane
The part of a cell's membrane that touches no other cell: the baseline of the enrichment.
Interface
The part of a cell's membrane within the interface width (Membrane / interface width) of a partner cell.
Marker of interest (MOI)
The marker whose enrichment at the interface is measured.
Neighbour track
For every position along a cell's membrane, the cell that touches it there (or none).
Partner preference
Contacts between two cell types observed ÷ expected by chance, within events of three or more cells.
Pool
The datasets that are classified together: one clustering and one set of thresholds.
Project
Exports, channel names and roles, and settings, saved as project.toml, with the results of all datasets.
Subtype marker
A marker (role Subtype) that is positive or negative per immune cell; the positive markers name the subtype.
Touching
Two cells of one event within the interface width of each other.
